title: I Took the CNC-Router Bit Checkout to the Intern Who Skipped the Tool Log

parts.text: I stepped into router one at 9:08 a.m. and intern Tess was already using my numbered bit. The board said: SIXTY MINUTES. BITS STAY IN THE LOG. I was thirty-three, shop lead, holding a clipboard that listed our job. Tess shrugged. "Interns learn the spindle." I photographed the board, the booking, and her collet on my bit. Then I asked for the tool log. At 9:16 the cnc desk pinged why Tess's collet sat on our bit. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The CNC desk can see Tess's collet on router one during our job.

social.video_title: She skipped the tool log on my numbered bit — Part 1/2
social.description: CNC router, an intern on my bit, a sixty-minute clock she posted. I logged the collet. Would you have asked for the tool log?

parts.text: Tess called it air cuts until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the collet still. The bit went back to my numbered foam. Tess ran a slot of their own and told the next intern atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: INTERNS DO NOT LEARN ON A BOOKED SPINDLE. I keep our job on a labeled card. Tess brown-bags her collets. The router finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Interns do not learn on a booked spindle — Part 2/2
social.description: Tool log, numbered bit, and a second line on the board. Were air cuts ever our job?
